sections.lesson_title: Using Properties Instead of Recomputing Integrals
sections.section_title: Introduction to Using Properties Instead of Recomputing Integrals

blocks.text: You already know the Fourier-series property formulas. In this lesson, the job is not to re-integrate; it is to inspect a transformed periodic signal with known $c_k$ and reuse the matching property or property chain to update the coefficients directly.

Scan the signal statement for the cue: time shift, time scaling, time reversal, vertical offset, or real-signal symmetry. If the signal has more than one change, chain the matching properties in the same order as the transformations instead of starting over with the coefficient integral.

For a single shift, every harmonic coefficient changes by the corresponding phase rule; for a vertical shift, only the DC term changes. When the signal is real, use symmetry to fill the negative indices instead of recomputing them.

Use the quick check: ask what changes in $c_k$, what changes only in $c_0$, and when negative coefficients come from symmetry. If you can answer those three questions, you can update the coefficients directly and avoid recomputing the coefficient integral.

sections.lesson_title: Using Properties Instead of Recomputing Integrals
sections.section_title: Selecting the Property from a Transformed Signal

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has known coefficients $c_k$. The new signal is $y(t)=x(-t)$. Decide which Fourier-series property applies and state how the coefficient indices change.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is the minus sign inside the argument: $y(t)=x(-t)$. That tells you the signal has been time-reversed, so the property to select is the time-reversal property rather than a shift or a scaling.

Read that rule as an index swap: the new coefficient at harmonic $k$ is the old coefficient at harmonic $-k$. Because this example contains only time reversal, you stop here and do not recompute the coefficient integral.

sections.lesson_title: Using Properties Instead of Recomputing Integrals
sections.section_title: Updating Known Coefficients with One Fourier Series Property

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$. Find the coefficients of $y(t)=x(t-t_0)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the delay inside $y(t)=x(t-t_0)$. That tells you to use the time-shift property, so each Fourier-series coefficient keeps its magnitude and picks up a harmonic-dependent phase factor.

So the update is coefficient-by-coefficient: multiply every $c_k$ by $e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$ and leave the magnitudes unchanged. The $k=0$ term stays the same, and no coefficient integral is recomputed.

sections.lesson_title: Using Properties Instead of Recomputing Integrals
sections.section_title: Combining a Time Shift with a Vertical Shift

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$. Find the coefficients of $y(t)=x(t-t_0)+A$.

explanation_blocks.text: The delay inside $x(t-t_0)$ is the first cue. Apply the time-shift property to the known coefficients before you handle the constant offset.
Then add the vertical shift. The constant $A$ changes only the DC term, so $d_0=\tilde c_0+A=c_0+A$ while every $k\neq 0$ coefficient stays equal to the time-shifted value.

The update is ordered and local: first update every coefficient by the time-shift rule, then change only the DC term by the vertical offset. That keeps the combined transformation from turning into a recomputation.

sections.section_title: Combining Time Reversal with Time Scaling

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$ and period $T$. Determine the coefficients and new fundamental period of $y(t)=x(-2t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the negative scale in $x(-2t)$. Treat it as a time reversal together with a factor-2 compression of the time axis.
Once the new period is fixed, use the reversal rule on the coefficient sequence. The harmonic index order flips, so the coefficient at index $k$ comes from the old coefficient at $-k$.
So the update is complete: halve the period, double the fundamental angular frequency, and read the coefficient list backward. No coefficient integral is recomputed.

sections.section_title: Using Conjugate Symmetry to Complete Coefficient Updates

example_content.example_prompt: A real periodic signal has updated positive-harmonic coefficients after a transformation. Use conjugate symmetry to determine the missing negative-index coefficients and complete the spectrum.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the signal is real after the transformation. That means the completed Fourier-series coefficients must satisfy conjugate symmetry.
So after you update the positive harmonics, fill each missing negative coefficient by conjugating the matching positive one. Leave the DC term real, and do not recompute any integrals.
That completes the spectrum directly from the known positive side: mirror the indices, apply conjugation, and keep the zero-frequency term real.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has known coefficients $c_k$. The new signal is $y(t)=x(-t)$. Which Fourier-series property applies and what is the coefficient-index rule?

choice_blocks.text: Time scaling, the period changes but the harmonic-index mapping does not

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The minus sign inside the argument is the cue for time reversal, not shift or scaling.
So the new coefficient at harmonic $k$ is the old coefficient at harmonic $-k$.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has known coefficients $c_k$. The new signal is $y(t)=x(-t)+A$. Which property combination applies before any coefficient arithmetic?

choice_blocks.text: Time reversal plus vertical shift, with the index reversal and a DC offset change
Time shift plus vertical shift, with a phase factor on every coefficient and a DC offset change
Time scaling only, with a new period but no index swap
Vertical shift only, with only $d_0$ changing

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The minus sign inside the argument still signals time reversal, and the added constant is a vertical shift.
So you combine the reversal rule with the fact that only the DC term changes for the vertical shift.

sections.section_title: Updating Known Coefficients with One Fourier Series Property

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$. The new signal is $y(t)=x(t-t_0)$. Which formula gives the coefficients $d_k$ of $y(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The delay in $x(t-t_0)$ is the cue for the time-shift property. Every coefficient keeps its magnitude and picks up the phase factor $e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$, so the correct rule is $d_k = c_k e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$. The new signal is $y(t)=x(t+t_0)$. Which formula gives the coefficients $d_k$ of $y(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The plus sign in $x(t+t_0)$ means an advance, which is the same time-shift property with the opposite exponent sign. So each coefficient is multiplied by $e^{jk\omega_0 t_0}$.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$. For $y(t)=x(t+t_0)-A$, which coefficient rule is correct?

choice_blocks.text: $d_0 = c_0 - A$, $d_k = c_k e^{jk\omega_0 t_0}$ for $k\neq 0$.
$d_0 = c_0 + A$, $d_k = c_k e^{jk\omega_0 t_0}$ for $k\neq 0$.
$d_0 = c_0 - A$, $d_k = c_k e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$ for $k\neq 0$.
$d_0 = c_0$, $d_k = c_k e^{jk\omega_0 t_0} - A$ for all $k$.

questions.correct_answer: $d_0 = c_0 - A$, $d_k = c_k e^{jk\omega_0 t_0}$ for $k\neq 0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The signal is advanced inside $x(t+t_0)$, so the Fourier-series time-shift rule multiplies each coefficient by $e^{jk\omega_0 t_0}$. The vertical shift $-A$ changes only the DC term, so subtract $A$ from $d_0$ and leave the nonzero harmonics at their shifted values.

prompt_blocks.text: A periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$. For $y(t)=x(t-t_0)-A$, which coefficient rule is correct?

choice_blocks.text: $d_0 = c_0 - A$, $d_k = c_k e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$ for $k\neq 0$.
$d_0 = c_0 + A$, $d_k = c_k e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$ for $k\neq 0$.
$d_0 = c_0 - A$, $d_k = c_k e^{jk\omega_0 t_0}$ for $k\neq 0$.
$d_0 = c_0$, $d_k = c_k e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0} - A$ for all $k$.

questions.correct_answer: $d_0 = c_0 - A$, $d_k = c_k e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$ for $k\neq 0$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The delay inside $x(t-t_0)$ triggers the time-shift rule, which multiplies each coefficient by $e^{-jk\omega_0 t_0}$. The vertical shift $-A$ changes only the DC term, so the final update is the shifted coefficient rule with $A$ subtracted from $d_0$.

prompt_blocks.text: If a periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$ and period $T$, which statement gives the coefficients and new fundamental period of $y(t)=x(-t/3)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The factor $1/3$ stretches the time axis by $3$, so the new period is $3T$. The minus sign reverses the harmonic index, so the coefficient rule is $d_k=c_{-k}$.

prompt_blocks.text: If a periodic signal $x(t)$ has coefficients $c_k$ and period $T$, which statement gives the coefficients and new fundamental period of $y(t)=x(-3t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The factor $3$ compresses the time axis by $3$, so the new period is $T/3$. The minus sign still flips the harmonic index, so $d_k=c_{-k}$.

prompt_blocks.text: A real periodic signal has updated coefficients $d_0=4$, $d_2=3-j$, and $d_5=-2j$ after a property update. Which completed coefficient set is correct?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Because the signal is real, use conjugate symmetry to fill the missing negative-harmonic coefficients, and keep $d_0$ real.

prompt_blocks.text: A real periodic signal has updated coefficients $d_0=7$, $d_1=1-3j$, and $d_4=2$ after a property update. Which completed coefficient set is correct?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use conjugate symmetry again because the signal is real. The DC coefficient stays real, and each negative-harmonic coefficient is the conjugate of the matching positive one.
